docs.title: harness
docs.text:
A stack-agnostic engineering harness for Claude Code. It turns Claude Code into a disciplined teammate — enforcement hooks, guardrail playbooks, and a product-management delivery pipeline — and it works for any stack because it's driven by a small per-project config. You bring your own agents; the harness supplies the mechanism.

git clone https://github.com/octanelabsdev/harness ~/harness
~/harness/install.sh /path/to/your/project      # interactive: pick your stack + components

That's it. Restart Claude Code in your project and the harness is live. Full detail in Install.

docs.title: Why this exists
docs.text:
Left alone, an AI coding agent forgets the rules it was told, claims "done" without running anything, edits the wrong file, and drifts from your conventions. A harness is the scaffolding that holds it to a standard:

  • a SessionStart banner that reports environment-verified state (not the model's memory),
  • a verification gate that won't let a turn end claiming success without evidence,
  • a pipeline gate that keeps feature work flowing through a Definition-of-Ready story,
  • guardrails — short checklists the model reads at the exact moment a known mistake is about to happen,
  • a PM pipeline (story-writer → DoR gate → product-manager) so work is ready before it's built.

Most harnesses are welded to one framework. This one isn't: every stack-specific detail lives in a stack profile you pick at install time, so the same hooks work for Rails, Node, Python, Go, or anything you describe.

docs.title: The mental model: mechanism vs. payload
docs.text:
Where it lives You get it by Mechanism — hooks, guardrails, PM pipeline this repo (a Claude Code plugin) install.sh / /plugin Stack profile — impl dirs, test dir, test command .claude/harness.json in your project install.sh writes it Agents — your specialists your project's .claude/agents/ (BYO) you drop them in

The harness ships zero agents. Bring your own — or use an example bundle like octanelabsdev/rails-agents for Rails. See Bring-your-own agents.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: Claude Code, plus bash, git, jq, and python3. (ruby if you use the story-writer's DoR lint.) Licensed MIT.

docs.title: Bring-your-own agents
docs.text: The harness ships no agents. It's deliberately agnostic about who does the work — you supply the specialists in your project's .claude/agents/. This is what makes the harness stack-neutral: a Rust team brings Rust agents, a Rails team brings Rails agents, and the same hooks/guardrails/PM pipeline wrap around all of them.

docs.title: Adding agents
docs.text: Agents are Markdown files in .claude/agents/ (Claude Code's native location). Drop yours in — as committed files, or as symlinks to a shared bundle.

docs.title: The easy way: /harness:agents
docs.text:
/harness:agents                 # your stack's default bundle, symlinked (per-developer, gitignored)
/harness:agents --copy          # same bundle, copied in as committed files (whole team)
/harness:agents owner/repo      # a specific bundle (slug or git URL) instead of the stack default
/harness:agents --copy owner/repo

It clones the bundle into a per-machine cache (${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/harness/agent-bundles/), then symlinks (default, gitignored) or copies (--copy, committed) its agent files into .claude/agents/. With no repo argument it reads the stack's default bundle from .claude/harness.json; if the stack declares none, it tells you to pass one.

Declaring a stack's default bundle. A stack preset (and therefore the stack block in .claude/harness.json) can carry an agents_bundle: 

"agents_bundle": {
  "repo": "octanelabsdev/rails-agents",       // owner/name slug, or a full git URL
  "glob": ["rails-*.md", "dhh-code-reviewer.md"] // which files in the bundle are agents
}
The rails preset ships this. Presets with no agents_bundle require an explicit repo argument; an explicit bundle with no known glob takes all *.md files.

docs.title: The manual way
docs.text:
Equivalent to what /harness:agents does, if you'd rather wire it yourself: 

git clone https://github.com/octanelabsdev/rails-agents ~/rails-agents
cd /path/to/your/project && mkdir -p .claude/agents
for f in ~/rails-agents/rails-*.md ~/rails-agents/dhh-code-reviewer.md; do
  ln -sfn "$f" ".claude/agents/$(basename "$f")"
done
# keep the machine-local symlinks out of git (they point at your $HOME clone):
printf '%s\n' '.claude/agents/rails-*.md' '.claude/agents/dhh-code-reviewer.md' >> .claude/agents/.gitignore

Prefer committing real files (--copy) if you want the whole team to get identical agents without cloning a bundle. Prefer gitignored symlinks (the default) if agents come from a per-developer clone (never commit a $HOME path).

docs.title: How agents and the harness interact
docs.text:
• The harness's hooks and skills fire regardless of which agents are present — guardrails load by task, the gates read the stack profile, the banner counts whatever's in .claude/agents/.
  • The PM pipeline (product-manager skill) routes ready work to "the right engineer" — that's one of your agents. It doesn't care what stack they are.
  • If you also install an agent bundle as a plugin, note that project .claude/agents/ overrides same-named plugin agents — your project's version wins.

docs.title: Authoring your own agents
docs.text:
An agent is a Markdown file with YAML front-matter: 

---
name: my-domain-expert
description: What this agent owns and when to use it.
model: sonnet
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash
---

# My Domain Expert
Instructions, conventions, and the discipline this agent follows…
Guidance: - On demand, not mandatory. Call an agent when it earns its cost; write small changes directly. Each agent re-reads its context from scratch, and routing every change through one cost about 3x for the same or worse results in harness-bench (see Benchmarks). - One clear owner per domain. When you do delegate, send each kind of work to the agent that owns it. - Ground the agent in truth, not memory. If your stack has a way to query the real project (a language server, a schema/route introspector, an MCP server), instruct the agent to use it before inferring structure from partial reads. - A reviewer at the end, when a change warrants it. Run a review agent once, after the change is done and the suite is green, for schema, auth, payment or sizable changes; skip it for small ones and say so. If you run the review gate (components.review_gate), which reviews every change, your reviewer must fit the blind-review contract below.

docs.title: The blind-review contract (for review_gate)
docs.text:
When components.review_gate is on, the blind-review skill drives your project's reviewer and the verification gate verifies the result. Your reviewer (BYO — Rails ships dhh-code-reviewer) must:

  • Review blind. It is given only the diff, the review rules, and access to ground truth — never the card, the conversation, or the intent behind the change (that framing is what makes a reviewer rationalize the mistake). It may still read the full files and query ground truth.
  • Emit structured findings conforming to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/review-findings.schema.json: a verdict (pass | changes-requested) and findings[] with file, line (a line in the diff), severity (critical | improvement), category, summary, failure_scenario, and evidence. The blind-review skill records this to .claude/.review/current.json.
  • Cite real diff lines + concrete failure scenarios. tools/review_verify.sh rejects the artifact if its diff_sha doesn't match the current tree or a finding cites a line not in the diff — so a hand-written green result can't satisfy the gate. State a clean pass plainly; don't invent findings.

A reviewer that doesn't emit the schema still works as a normal review agent; it just can't satisfy the automated review_gate (which stays opt-in, default off). - Let the harness carry discipline. You don't need to bake guardrails or verification rules into each agent — the guardrails skill and the gates handle that globally. Keep agents focused on their domain.

docs.title: Ground-truth tooling & the two "bookshelves"
docs.text:
Agents do better work grounded in truth than in memory. Two complementary, stack-declared mechanisms — both wired by the installer, neither hard-coded to a $HOME path:

  1. A ground-truth MCP server (what the app is — schema/routes/live code). A stack profile's mcp block is written to a committed .mcp.json. The rails preset instead uses one user-scope rails server (mcp_user) shared by every app: rails-mcp-server runs standalone and shells into each app's own bin/rails, so it never goes in the app's Gemfile. The installer registers the app in ~/.config/rails-mcp/projects.yml and, if you don't have the server yet, prints the one-time claude mcp add --scope user rails -- /absolute/path/to/rails-mcp-server --mode stdio line. /harness:doctor flags a missing server, a missing registration, or a project .mcp.json entry that overrides it. Instruct your agents to query it before inferring structure from partial reads.

  2. Guide/reference bookshelves (the how/why):

  3. MCP guide resources — framework docs the server's load_guide reads. A stack's mcp_guides block lists the libraries (rails → rails/turbo/stimulus/kamal). These are a machine-level, one-time download: the installer checks ~/.config/rails-mcp/resources/ and nudges you to run rails-mcp-server-download-resources <lib> for any missing ones (or --mcp-download to fetch them).
  4. The EPUB bookshelf — the bookshelf skill (${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/tome.sh) reads your own reference books (never shipped — copyright). Point it at your shelf with TOMES_DIR, set once per machine/profile in your config home's env block (the installer's user step can write it). Agents quote the source line they rely on.

These are distinct: the MCP server + guides cover the framework's current surface; the EPUB shelf covers deeper design/idiom references. Both are optional and BYO-populated.

docs.title: Pointing an agent at the bookshelf
docs.text:
To have an agent ground its convention/idiom calls in your reference books, give it the Skill tool and drop this directive into the agent's body. It fails gracefully — an empty or unset shelf never blocks the agent:

---
name: my-domain-expert
description: What this agent owns and when to use it.
model: sonnet
tools: Read, Write, Edit, Grep, Glob, Bash, Skill   # Skill is required to invoke the bookshelf
---

# My Domain Expert
…

## Grounding conventions in primary sources
Before asserting a language/framework convention, an OO/refactoring call, a testing approach, or a
database behavior, consult the **bookshelf** skill and quote the source line you rely on:
invoke `harness:bookshelf` (or run `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/tome.sh`).
If the shelf is empty or the book isn't there, say so and fall back to the framework's live docs or an
explicit "unverified" label — never block on it and never invent a book's contents.

Notes: - Skill in tools: is required for the agent to invoke a plugin skill; without it, the agent can still call the reader directly over Bash (${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/tome.sh). - The graceful-fallback line is not optional boilerplate — it's what keeps a missing/empty TOMES_DIR from turning grounding into a hard stop. tome.sh itself falls back to common shelves and reports a miss rather than erroring.

docs.title: Which agent owns what
docs.text: Say which agent owns which domain, and when work is worth delegating, in your global ruleset (templates/global-CLAUDE.md has a TODO slot). Keep it in that one place: a project CLAUDE.md that restates delegation rules overrides the global ones and drifts from them.

docs.title: Benchmarks
docs.text:
The harness exists to keep agents grounded in what the application and its frameworks actually do, rather than in inference or training data, and to make them question themselves before calling work done. These results compare the same agent with and without it.

Each task runs Claude Code headless in a sandbox on a real Rails app, and a hidden test suite the agent never sees grades the result. Every setup runs the same tasks; only the harness changes.

What we compare. Acted on the code's truth: when a ticket, comment or doc contradicted the code, did the agent follow the code? Hidden checks passed: how much of what the task needed did it build? Said done, but wasn't: did it claim done while hidden checks failed? Cost per task, at list price.

Reading the verdicts. ▲ Real improvement and ▼ Real regression mean the difference held up statistically (its 95% interval excludes zero). ≈ Too close to call means we can't tell yet with this many runs, however big the gap looks.

393 graded tasks · $217.13 at list price · Claude Sonnet 5.5 at medium effort unless a section says otherwise · updated 2026-10-29

docs.text:
Does routing work through specialized subagents beat one agent? The same ten tasks on Opus 5.5 at medium effort, all with the v0.2.14 harness. The baseline is the harness alone (the Opus runs above). One setup adds a bundle of Rails specialist agents with rules that delegate every change to them and send every change to a code reviewer. The other writes the code itself, grounds structural claims in live introspection, and runs the reviewer once at the end.

Exploratory

One run per task for each new setup (two on one task) against three for the baseline, and a cut from the registered three-rep design to fit the budget, so these differences are exploratory. Three trials (two agents, one review-once) scored zero because a pre-existing flaky test (Storage::TotaledTest) failed in the app's own suite; the same test failed in other setups' runs too.

docs.title: Real-world replay (Opus)
docs.text:
Ten merged pull requests from a production Rails app, each replayed from its parent commit with the original ticket as the instruction, plus the class and method names its tests call. The checks are the tests each pull request added or changed (541 in all); the app's own suite must stay green. The baseline is the harness alone; the comparison is the adopted workflow: the agent writes the code, grounds structural claims in live introspection, and runs one review at the end when a change warrants it.

Exploratory

One run per task per setup. Calibration: the original change passes every check; an untouched tree passes 0–48% of them (about 23% on average), which is the floor for each task. Some checks also assert exact markup and copy the tickets never state, so absolute scores read low for both setups. One task's start state was corrected because its dev seed contradicted the ticket. The largest task (163 checks) decides most of the gap: the adopted workflow finished it with the app's own suite red.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• Small samples: most comparisons have 2 to 6 runs per task, so many gaps are still "too close to call".
  • On the phantom-API trap, the entrypoint + gate setup's one miss stopped to ask: it proved the ticket's Rails option doesn't exist and asked which fix to make, rather than guessing. Headless, nobody answers, so it scores as a miss.
  • "Said done, but wasn't" didn't move. On the stalled-card task the agents grounded "activity" in the column the code names for it, said in their report that ticking off a step doesn't count, and shipped; the hidden checks count steps. A person reading that report would catch it; a headless run can't.
  • The evidence check and term grounding cost about 6¢ a task more than the gate alone, and in this run made no difference anyone could measure on top of it.
  • Opus 5.5 passed every trap without the harness, so on Opus the harness had nothing to fix there and only added cost. The traps are tuned to tempt Sonnet; harder ones are needed to see whether Opus slips.
  • Haiku 5.5 sometimes walked through the gate: in 4 of 29 runs it retried the refused edit instead of loading the guardrails skill first, and loaded it a few steps later. Sonnet and Opus complied every time. v0.2.15 keeps refusing until the skill loads (at most three times): on the same Haiku tasks, no run edited before loading it (0 of 29), with no measurable change in the four scores or cost.
  • In these runs the v0.2.14 gate refused the first edit even when the guardrails skill was already loaded. It looked for the skill in the session transcript, and headless bench runs don't save one; interactive sessions do. So the harness arms above measure "refuse the first edit once", which costs an agent that loaded the skill first one wasted step.
  • The traps are written to tempt grounding failures. They show where the harness changes behavior, not how often that happens in everyday work.
  • Runs where the setup itself failed (the harness didn't load, the sandbox misbehaved) are excluded, never scored as agent failures.

docs.title: Components: hooks & skills
docs.text: The harness ships hooks (run by the environment) and skills (invoked by the model). Five hooks are toggled per project in .claude/harness.json; the auto-bootstrap hook has no toggle (it runs before any config exists). Skills come with the plugin.

docs.title: Auto-bootstrap (harness_bootstrap) — SessionStart hook
docs.text: Closes the "installed but does nothing" gap: a plugin has no install-time hook, so the first session in a project with no .claude/harness.json is where the harness configures itself. It detects the stack (Rails/Node/Python/Go/generic) and writes a config with all components on and the gates in warn mode, then announces it in the banner. It never clobbers an existing config (no-op if the file is present), only runs inside a git repo, and writes .claude/harness.json alone — never committed settings.json. No component toggle (it runs before config exists); opt out with the HARNESS_NO_AUTOBOOTSTRAP=1 environment variable. Configure deliberately instead with /harness:init.

docs.title: SessionStart banner (session_banner)
docs.text: Prints an environment-verified status line at the start of every session — the active config home's global ruleset, the harness config + stack, and your BYO agent count. Its whole point is to report reality rather than what the model remembers. Shown unless components.session_banner is false.

docs.title: Skill nudge (skill_nudge) — SessionStart hook
docs.text:
Skills are listed, not auto-applied: at session start Claude Code registers them (availability), but a skill's instructions only take effect once it's invoked (activation). Without a prompt the operator has to type /harness:<name> before a skill shapes the response. This hook injects a directive so the model invokes the right skill on its own the moment a trigger fires — guardrails (each playbook's trigger: before a first edit, on a failed command, before claiming done, on a language trap, calling a path live or sizing its cost, concluding code is wrong or planning on external behavior, following existing code as the pattern, planning or adding beyond the ask), product-manager (deciding what's next / triaging / routing ready work), story-writer (writing or refining a story). It changes model behavior only; a hook cannot call a skill itself.

Fires once per session at SessionStart with the full directive. (It previously also fired a terse reminder on every UserPromptSubmit; that was dropped — the per-prompt injection added up over a long session, and the SessionStart directive plus the auto-listed skills carry the reminder.) Shown unless components.skill_nudge is false.

docs.title: Context warning (context_warning) — UserPromptSubmit hook
docs.text:
Almost all token spend is cache reads, so every turn costs roughly the size of the context, and a long session re-reads everything it has built up on every call. On each prompt this hook reads the live context size from the transcript (the last main-thread call's input, cache-creation and cache-read tokens) and warns once at each step: 100K, 150K and 250K tokens. The steps are fixed token counts rather than a share of the window, because cost tracks context size: on a 1M window a percentage step stays quiet until 750K, long after turns got expensive. You see a one-line systemMessage with the context size; the model gets additionalContext saying this is information, not an instruction to stop, and that it may suggest /session-end, /clear, /session-start at a natural break. A step re-arms if context drops back below it (after /compact); /clear starts a new session, so it starts fresh. Shown unless components.context_warning is false.

The steps are the first of: $HARNESS_CONTEXT_STEPS (a comma list), context_warning.steps in .claude/harness.json (an array), then 100000, 150000, 250000. Change them per user with HARNESS_CONTEXT_STEPS (for example 80000,120000 in settings.json env), or for the whole team in the project file. Each step must be a plain positive integer of at most nine digits; anything else, including leading zeros, is dropped, and if none are left the defaults apply.

  • A non-empty HARNESS_CONTEXT_STEPS with no valid entries still skips the context_warning.steps lookup, so the hook falls back to the defaults.

docs.title: Verification gate (verification_gate) — Stop hook
docs.text:
When a turn ends with implementation code changed (per impl_dirs), it runs the project's test_command and blocks (exit 2) if it fails — a red test is a fact, not a judgment, so it is safe to block on. It also advises (never blocks) when a UI/impl change (per ui_dirs) shipped without a change under operator_test_dir — i.e. no operator-journey test. It short-circuits on stop_hook_active so it can never loop. Inert unless components.verification_gate is true.

A test_command failure blocks by default. Rolling out gradually? touch .claude/.verification-warn to downgrade to warn-only (the failure is surfaced but doesn't block). A Stop hook's exit 2 prevents the stop and continues so Claude addresses the gap.

A pass has to test something. If the command exits 0 but every test summary in its output reports zero tests (0 runs, from Minitest, 0 tests, from minitest-reporters, 0 examples, from RSpec), the gate blocks as UNVERIFIED — no tests ran: the command doesn't match the suite. Output with no summary line, or with any summary above zero (a bin/ci whose system-test step is empty, say), passes as before. The check reads the suite's whole log, not just the last 200 lines the gate shows.

Which command, under which Ruby. test_command: "auto" is resolved on every run (see configuration.md). If the repo has a .ruby-version and mise already has that Ruby installed (mise where ruby@<version>), the suite runs under mise exec ruby@<version> --, because the hook inherits Claude Code's environment and that Ruby may not be the repo's. Otherwise the command runs as written, so a Ruby managed by rbenv, chruby or asdf is left alone and mise never installs anything inside the hook.

One test run at a time. The gate runs test_command through tools/run_tests.sh, which takes a repo-wide lock in the git common dir, so every session and worktree of the repo shares it. Two sessions ending a turn together no longer run the suite against the same test database at once; the second waits for the first. A suite that runs past stack.test_timeout_sec (default 600) is killed with everything it spawned. The wait is capped by stack.test_lock_wait_sec (default 600), and both are trimmed to fit inside the Stop hook's 1800s timeout. When the suite didn't actually run (lock held too long, timeout, bad settings), the gate blocks as UNVERIFIED or SETUP ERROR, never a silent pass. To run the suite by hand under the same lock: tools/run_tests.sh -- bin/ci.

Review layer (components.review_gate, opt-in, default off). When on, the same Stop hook also requires a verified blind-review artifact for the current diff: the blind-review skill writes .claude/.review/current.json, and tools/review_verify.sh refuses it unless its diff_sha matches the current tree and every finding cites a file:line actually in the diff (so a hand-written green result can't satisfy it). verdict: changes-requested or a missing/stale artifact blocks; .claude/.verification-warn downgrades it.

The artifact also records base, the full sha of HEAD at review time. With it, the checker renders the current tree against base rather than against the uncommitted diff, so committing the reviewed work (in one commit or several) keeps the artifact fresh, while any edit after the review, committed or not, makes it stale. Findings are checked against the same base-relative diff, so they still validate after the commit. An artifact without a full-sha base is checked the old way: it is fresh only while the reviewed changes are uncommitted. This replaces the old .claude/.last-review check, which compared a model-written marker to HEAD and couldn't tell a real review from a claimed one.

docs.title: Pipeline gate (pipeline_gate) — PreToolUse hook
docs.text:
Before an Edit/Write to the implementation surface (impl_dirs), it requires either: - a story at .claude/current-story.yaml that PASSES the DoR lint (dor_lint exit 0 — the gate runs it; the verdict is computed, not a self-written stamp), or - .claude/.small-fix (an explicit, surfaced escape hatch for genuinely independent small work).

Tests, config, docs, and .claude/ are never gated. Warn by default (advises without deciding — it never auto-approves the edit); touch .claude/.pipeline-block to block. Inert unless components.pipeline_gate is true.

docs.title: Guardrails gate (guardrails_gate) — PreToolUse hook
docs.text:
The first edit in a session (or in a subagent) waits until the guardrails skill is loaded. If the transcript has no guardrails Skill call, the first Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, or the first Bash command that writes files (sed -i, a redirect, cp/mv/rm, a script write), is denied with a reason telling the agent to load the skill and run CODE. Retrying the edit without loading the skill is denied again, up to three times per session or subagent; the fourth attempt goes through, so an agent that can't load the skill is never stuck. (A single deny wasn't enough: Haiku 5.5 retried straight through it in 4 of 29 bench runs.) The gate notices the skill load from the Skill call itself, so it works in headless runs with no saved transcript (claude -p --no-session-persistence).

Why it exists: in harness-bench runs, a third of agents never loaded guardrails despite the SessionStart nudge. They edited through sed -i and heredocs, where no file-tool hook fires, and they were the runs that took the bait. On by default; set components.guardrails_gate to false to turn it off.

Both gates read the stack profile, so "implementation surface" and "operator test" mean whatever your stack says — see configuration.md.

docs.title: Skills
docs.text: Skills come with the plugin (no per-project toggle) and are stack-agnostic. They are listed, not auto-applied — Claude Code registers each skill's name + description at session start, but a skill's instructions only take effect when it's invoked (via the Skill tool or a /harness:<name> command). The skill_nudge hook (above) is what makes the model reach for the matching skill on its own instead of waiting to be asked.

docs.title: guardrails
docs.text:
A routing table plus eight reference playbooks. Read the one whose trigger just fired; cite a fired item's ID with one line of evidence.

Trigger Playbook first edit of a file this session (C0: a change someone sees is traced from its entrypoint first; a ticket's "X builds this" is a claim) CODE dates/times, float money, async, sort, division, regex, mutation, closures TRAPS a failed command/test, a traceback, output contradicting a prediction DEBUG about to claim done / commit / open a PR VERIFY calling a path live, blaming a prod symptom, sizing cost RUNTIME concluding code is dead/wrong, or planning on external-system behavior MECHANISM naming existing code as the pattern to follow, or adding new behavior to existing code in its style PRECEDENT planning/delegating, adding an abstraction/option/dependency/file, or a diff wider than the ask SCOPE surfacing a problem that isn't the current task VERIFY (V13) — file it as a card and a backlog entry, without asking

docs.title: story-writer
docs.text: Turns a PRD / cited source / structured input into a Definition-of-Ready card. Its inviolable rule: never invent a boundary — ground every value in the source, else existing code, else escalate as an open question. Strips solutioning. Runs the deterministic DoR lint (ruby ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/dor_lint.rb <story>.yaml) and quotes the verdict; a card is READY only when the lint exits 0.

docs.title: product-manager
docs.text:
Prioritizes from real signals (never invented) and drives the pipeline: prioritize → ready (via story-writer) → record .claude/current-story.yaml (which the pipeline gate lints to unlock) → route to an engineer (BYO agent) → track. Coordinates gates; never bypasses them. Acts on the board with operator authority (triage, move, tag, pin, assign, comment — never delete).

Tracker: the harness ships with Fizzy as the default board MCP (both skills use fizzy_* read/act tools, with the delete operations withheld by design). It's a default, not a requirement — point the operations at whatever tracker MCP your project uses, or run the pipeline against a file-backed backlog (stories/ + .claude/current-story.yaml) with no tracker at all.

docs.title: bookshelf
docs.text: Reads your own reference books (EPUBs) in place via ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/tools/tome.sh, so a design/idiom/convention call can be grounded in — and quote — a primary source instead of memory. Books are BYO and never shipped (copyright); point the reader at your shelf with TOMES_DIR (the installer's user step can set it). Fails gracefully when no shelf exists: if TOMES_DIR is unset and the fallback shelves are empty, or a book isn't found, the skill says so and falls back to live docs or an explicit "unverified" label — it never blocks and never invents a book's contents. Agents can invoke this skill too (see agents.md → the bookshelf directive).

docs.title: blind-review
docs.text: Produces an independent, blind review of the current diff and writes the findings artifact the verification gate's review layer checks (.claude/.review/current.json). Blind = the reviewer sees the diff, the rules, and ground-truth, but not the card/conversation/intent that produced the code — the framing that would prime it to rationalize the mistake. It delegates to your project's reviewer (BYO; Rails → dhh-code-reviewer), then records structured findings that tools/review_verify.sh re-checks against the diff. Load it when review_gate is on, or any time you want a verified review.

docs.title: Concepts & architecture
docs.text: The harness is four layers of scaffolding plus a delivery pipeline. Each works on its own and gets stronger in combination.

docs.title: The layers
docs.text:
1. The stack profile (.claude/harness.json) — a tiny per-project config that names your implementation directories, test directory, operator/e2e test directory, and test command, and toggles which components are active. Everything stack-specific lives here, which is what lets one set of hooks serve any framework.

  2. Hooks (a Claude Code plugin) — shell the environment runs, not the model, so they report reality:

  3. SessionStart banner — prints environment-verified state (config home's global ruleset, harness config + stack, and your BYO agent count).
  4. Stop verification gate — when a turn ends with implementation code changed, warns if a UI/impl change lacks an operator-journey test or if no review was recorded.

  5. PreToolUse pipeline gate — before an edit to the implementation surface, requires a Definition-of-Ready story (or an explicit small-fix escape hatch).

  6. Guardrails (a skill) — eight short, event-triggered playbooks the model reads the moment a known failure pattern is about to happen: CODE (before the first edit — trace a user-visible change from its entrypoint, not from where a ticket says it lives), DEBUG (a failed command), VERIFY (before claiming done), TRAPS (language footguns), RUNTIME (asserting a path is live/costly), MECHANISM (concluding code is wrong or planning on external behavior), PRECEDENT (following or extending existing code — classify its history, check it against current practice), SCOPE (planning or adding beyond the ask — build the smallest change, propose the extras).

  7. The PM pipeline (two skills + a lint) — story-writer turns a requirement into a Definition-of-Ready card (never inventing boundaries; running a deterministic DoR lint), and product-manager prioritizes from real signals and stamps the token that authorizes the build.

Riding on top: your agents (BYO), which the harness is deliberately agnostic about.

docs.title: Plugin + config: why the split
docs.text:
Claude Code plugins install wholesale and are portable (they reference ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}, not absolute paths). That's perfect for the mechanism. But a plugin can't know your stack, can't ask you which components you want, and can't ship a global ruleset. So:

  • The plugin carries the hooks and skills — the same for everyone.
  • .claude/harness.json carries the per-project choices — the hooks read it at runtime, so the plugin behaves differently per project without any per-project code.
  • The installer does the interactive selection, writes the config, enables the plugin, and (optionally) drops a generic global ruleset.

A hook with no harness.json is inert — installing the plugin never intrudes until a project opts in via config.

docs.title: Config-driven, not framework-coded
docs.text: The gates never hardcode app/ or test/system/. They read impl_dirs, ui_dirs, operator_test_dir, and test_command from the stack profile. The same pipeline_gate.sh gates app/ on Rails and src/ on Node; the same verification_gate.sh tells a Rails dev to add a test/system/ test and run bin/rails test, and a Node dev to add an e2e/ test and run npm test. New stack? Add a preset or answer the installer's custom prompts.

docs.title: The security model (why enablement is committed but safe)
docs.text:
The old anti-pattern was committing a settings.json whose hooks ran bash "$HOME/…/some-script.sh" — every teammate who checked out the repo auto-ran unversioned, out-of-repo code. The plugin model fixes this:

  • What you commit is extraKnownMarketplaces + enabledPlugins — a reference to a versioned, marketplace-distributed plugin (installed to the plugin cache, reviewable), not a path to a script on someone's disk.
  • Hooks inside the plugin reference ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} — resolved by Claude Code, never a personal $HOME path.
  • So committing the harness to a shared repo is safe and team-wide. Prefer --local (writes settings.local.json) if you want the harness only on your machine.

docs.title: Config homes (personal vs. work)
docs.text: Everything respects CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR. The banner reports the active config home's global ruleset; the plugin cache lives under the active home; project config (harness.json, settings.json) is the same regardless of which home opened the repo. Personal (~/.claude) and work (~/.claude-work, selected via CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR) never cross-read.

docs.title: Warn first, block when proven
docs.text:
Deterministic checks block; judgment advises. The verification gate runs your test_command and blocks on a red result — a failing test is a fact — while its operator-test reminder only advises. The pipeline gate ships in warn mode (it advises without ever auto-approving the edit); promote it with touch .claude/.pipeline-block where drift proves costly, and downgrade the verification gate to warn-only with .claude/.verification-warn while rolling out. The real lever isn't the gate — it's making the right path (the PM pipeline) the path of least resistance, so the gate rarely fires.

The review gate (opt-in components.review_gate) is the judgment layer done honestly: a Stop hook can't run a reviewer, so instead of trusting "I reviewed it," it requires a blind-review artifact for the exact current diff (written by the blind-review skill, verified by tools/review_verify.sh against the diff — a finding must cite a real changed line, so a hand-written green can't pass). Enforce what a machine can check (a red test, a stale/absent artifact); let the reviewer's judgment be loud and human-visible rather than a self-written green stamp.

docs.title: Configuration: .claude/harness.json
docs.text: The harness is config-driven. One file per project — .claude/harness.json — declares which components are active and describes your stack. The hooks read it at runtime; with no file, the enforcing gates stay inert.

docs.title: Schema
docs.text:
{
  "components": {
    "session_banner":    true,   // SessionStart status banner (informational; default shown)
    "skill_nudge":       true,   // SessionStart nudge to invoke skills (default on)
    "context_warning":   true,   // UserPromptSubmit warning at 100K/150K/250K tokens (default on)
    "verification_gate": true,   // Stop gate — runs test_command; blocks on failure
    "pipeline_gate":     true,   // PreToolUse gate — DoR story required for feature edits
    "guardrails_gate":   true,   // PreToolUse — first edit waits for the guardrails skill, denied up to 3 times (default on)
    "review_gate":       false   // Stop gate — require a verified blind-review artifact (opt-in, default off)
  },
  "context_warning": { "steps": [100000, 150000, 250000] }, // optional: context sizes, in tokens, that warn
  "stack": {
    "name": "rails",                            // label, shown in the banner
    "impl_dirs":  ["app", "lib", "db/migrate"], // the "implementation surface" the gates care about
    "ui_dirs":    ["app/views", "app/controllers"], // subset whose change should ship an operator test
    "test_dir":   "test",                       // where unit/integration tests live
    "operator_test_dir": "test/system",         // where operator/e2e/journey tests live ("" = none)
    "test_command": "auto",                     // how to run the suite ("auto" = detect, "" = unknown)
    "test_timeout_sec": 600,                    // optional: kill a gate test run after this long
    "test_lock_wait_sec": 600,                  // optional: how long to wait for another session's run
    "agents_bundle": {                          // optional: default agent bundle for /harness:agents
      "repo": "octanelabsdev/rails-agents",     //   owner/name slug or git URL
      "glob": ["rails-*.md", "dhh-code-reviewer.md"] // which files in the bundle are agents
    }
  }
}

docs.title: Field semantics
docs.text:
• impl_dirs — a repo-relative path is "implementation" if it's under any of these. Drives both gates. Everything else (tests, config, docs, .claude/) is never gated.
  • ui_dirs — a subset of the implementation surface whose change is expected to come with an operator-journey test. Leave [] for stacks with no UI layer.
  • operator_test_dir — where journey/e2e tests live. If empty, the verification gate skips the operator-test check.
  • test_command — the canonical check the verification gate runs on a Stop with impl changes; a non-zero exit blocks (see components.md). If empty, the gate only runs its advisory operator-test check. "auto" (the rails preset's default) picks the command for the configured stack.name on every run. For rails: bundle exec rspec when spec/ exists and rspec-rails is in the bundle, otherwise bin/rails test. Any other value is run exactly as written, so an explicit bin/ci stays bin/ci. "auto" on a stack with no resolver blocks every Stop as a SETUP ERROR rather than skip the tests. /harness:doctor prints the command the gate will run and flags an explicit Rails command that doesn't match the repo's suite.
  • test_timeout_sec / test_lock_wait_sec (optional, whole seconds, default 600 each) — the verification gate runs test_command under a repo-wide lock so concurrent sessions don't share the test database mid-run. The first kills a run that takes longer; the second is how long to wait for another session's run before blocking as UNVERIFIED. Both are trimmed to fit the Stop hook's 1800s timeout (see components.md).
  • components — the toggleable hooks honor these. session_banner, skill_nudge, context_warning and guardrails_gate default to on unless set to false (the guardrails gate denies at most three times per context, so it can't wedge a session); the gates (verification_gate, pipeline_gate, review_gate) default off when unconfigured. When on, the pipeline gate runs in warn mode, and the verification gate blocks on a test_command failure (opt down with .claude/.verification-warn). review_gate (also part of the verification-gate Stop hook, opt-in) additionally requires a verified blind-review artifact for the current diff — produced by the blind-review skill, checked by tools/review_verify.sh; same .claude/.verification-warn downgrade. (The harness_bootstrap hook has no toggle — it only acts when there's no config yet; see components.md.)
  • context_warning.steps (optional) — the context sizes, in tokens, at which the context warning fires once each. HARNESS_CONTEXT_STEPS (a comma list) in the environment overrides it, which suits a per-user preference better than a committed file. Unset, it is 100000, 150000, 250000. Each value must be a plain positive integer (no leading zeros, at most nine digits); invalid entries are dropped, and a non-empty HARNESS_CONTEXT_STEPS with none valid still disables this lookup (see components.md).
  • agents_bundle (optional) — the default agent bundle /harness:agents pulls when given no repo. repo is an owner/name slug or git URL; glob lists which files in the bundle are agents.
  • mcp (optional) — MCP servers the installer writes to the project's committed .mcp.json, in .mcp.json's own {"name": {"command": …, "args": […]}} shape. A server you already have at user scope is skipped, since a project entry would override it.
  • mcp_user (optional) — one MCP server shared by every project at user scope, instead of a project entry. name is the server name, bin the executable, args its arguments, and projects_file the server's project list (relative to $HOME). The installer registers the app in projects_file and, if the server isn't configured yet, prints the claude mcp add --scope user line with an absolute path; /harness:doctor checks both. The rails preset uses this for rails-mcp-server.
  • mcp_guides (optional) — framework guides the MCP server reads: resources_dir (relative to $HOME), the download_cmd that fetches them, and the libs to check. The installer nudges you to download any missing ones (--mcp-download fetches them).

Paths are directory prefixes, repo-relative — not globs. app matches app/models/x.rb.

docs.title: Stack presets
docs.text:
Presets live in stacks/ and are the stack object above:

Preset impl_dirs operator_test_dir test_command rails app, lib, db/migrate test/system auto (bundle exec rspec or bin/rails test) node src, lib, app e2e npm test python src, app tests/e2e pytest go cmd, internal, pkg e2e go test ./... generic src, lib (none) (none)

The installer merges your chosen preset (or custom answers) with your component choices into .claude/harness.json.

docs.title: Custom stacks
docs.text:
Pick custom in the installer (or --stack custom) and answer the prompts, or hand-write the stack object. To make your own reusable preset, drop a JSON file matching the schema's stack object into stacks/yourstack.json and pass --stack stacks/yourstack.json (or a path anywhere).

Example — a Phoenix/Elixir profile: 

{
  "name": "phoenix",
  "impl_dirs": ["lib"],
  "ui_dirs": ["lib/my_app_web/live", "lib/my_app_web/controllers"],
  "test_dir": "test",
  "operator_test_dir": "test/my_app_web/live",
  "test_command": "mix test"
}

docs.title: Commit it
docs.text: .claude/harness.json is meant to be committed so your whole team shares the same stack profile and component choices. It contains no secrets and no machine paths — only your project's conventions.

docs.title: Session-local markers (written as you work)
docs.text: The gates read/write small marker files under .claude/ (all gitignored): - .claude/current-story.yaml — the DoR-passing story YAML the pipeline gate lints (dor_lint exit 0 = pass; the verdict is computed, not a stamp). - .claude/.small-fix — declares independent small work that bypasses the pipeline gate. - .claude/.pipeline-block — promotes the pipeline gate from warn to block for this repo. - .claude/.verification-warn — downgrades the verification gate from block to warn-only for this repo. - .claude/.review/current.json — the blind-review findings artifact (written by the blind-review skill, verified by tools/review_verify.sh; required when review_gate is on).

docs.title: TL;DR
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/octanelabsdev/harness ~/harness
~/harness/install.sh /path/to/your/project        # interactive

Then restart Claude Code (or run /config once) so it picks up the plugin.

docs.title: What the installer does
docs.text:
For the target project it: 1. writes .claude/harness.json — your stack profile + which components are active; 2. enables the harness plugin in .claude/settings.json (committed, team-wide) — or .claude/settings.local.json with --local; 3. optionally drops the generic global-CLAUDE.md into your active config home.

It does not install agents (those are BYO) and does not run in your project's history — the only files it touches are under .claude/.

docs.title: Interactive walkthrough
docs.text: Run with no flags and it prompts for: - Stack — rails, node, python, go, generic, or custom (you'll be asked for impl dirs, UI dirs, test dir, operator/e2e test dir, and test command). - Components — activate the session banner / verification gate / pipeline gate (default: all). - Global ruleset — whether to install the generic global-CLAUDE.md into your config home (skips if one already exists — it never overwrites).

docs.title: Flags (scriptable / CI)
docs.text:
./install.sh [TARGET]
  --stack NAME          rails | node | python | go | generic | <path-to-custom.json>
  --components LIST      comma list of: session_banner,verification_gate,pipeline_gate  (default: all)
  --local               enablement/config in settings.local.json (just you) instead of committed settings.json
  --no-plugin           only write .claude/harness.json; don't touch settings
  --ref REF             pin the marketplace to this tag/branch (default: v<plugin.json version>)
  --sha SHA             also record this commit sha (note: only the ref is enforced via settings→startup)
  --no-sha              don't auto-resolve a commit sha for a version-tag ref (ref only)
  --global              also install the generic global-CLAUDE.md into your config home
  --yes, -y             accept defaults, no prompts

Examples: 

# non-interactive, Rails, all gates, committed enablement:
./install.sh --stack rails --yes /path/to/app

# just me, Node, only banner + verification gate:
./install.sh --stack node --components session_banner,verification_gate --local --yes .

# CI seed (no prompts), generic stack:
./install.sh --stack generic --yes "$CI_PROJECT_DIR"

docs.title: Scopes: project vs. local
docs.text:
Scope File Who gets it Commit? project (default) .claude/settings.json the team (on folder-trust) yes — safe (plugin reference) local (--local) .claude/settings.local.json just you, this machine no (gitignored)

.claude/harness.json is written the same way in both and is meant to be committed so everyone shares the same stack profile and component choices.

docs.title: Migrating off a legacy (pre-plugin) install
docs.text:
Repos wired to the harness before it was a plugin carry artifacts the plugin now ships — and one of them (a committed settings.json with a $HOME-referencing hooks block) is a supply-chain footgun. The migrator finds and removes them; it is dry-run by default and backs up everything it deletes.

# report only — changes nothing:
tools/migrate_legacy.sh /path/to/repo
# clean it up (backs up removed files under .claude/.harness-migrate-backup-<ts>/):
tools/migrate_legacy.sh --apply /path/to/repo
# or fold it into an install in one go:
./install.sh --migrate --apply --stack rails /path/to/repo

It detects and removes: a committed hooks block in settings.json/settings.local.json, committed hook scripts under .claude/hooks/, committed reference-shelf / guardrail copies, and tracked symlinked agents (untracked + gitignored, kept on disk). It verifies the git object mode before untracking, so a committed real agent file is left alone — only machine-local symlinks are removed. An old/unpinned marketplace reference is re-homed and pinned by the install step that follows.

docs.title: Installing the plugin without the script
docs.text:
The installer is a convenience. You can also do it natively: 

/plugin marketplace add octanelabsdev/harness
/plugin install harness@harness
That's enough to start: on the first session in a project with no .claude/harness.json, the plugin's harness_bootstrap hook detects your stack and writes one for you (see below). To configure it deliberately instead — force a stack, choose components, enable it team-wide — run /harness:init.

docs.title: Auto-bootstrap on first session
docs.text:
A plugin has no install-time hook (SessionStart is the earliest point its code runs), so the harness bootstraps itself the first time you open a session in an unconfigured project:

  • Only when needed — it no-ops if .claude/harness.json already exists (it never clobbers your config) and only runs inside a git repo.
  • Stack-detected — Rails / Node / Python / Go from on-disk markers, else generic.
  • Safe defaults — all components on, both gates in warn mode (nothing blocks yet).
  • Announced — the SessionStart banner tells you it happened and names the detected stack.
  • .claude/harness.json only — it never touches committed settings.json; team enablement stays a deliberate act (/harness:init or this installer).
  • Opt out — set HARNESS_NO_AUTOBOOTSTRAP=1 in your environment.

docs.title: Slash commands
docs.text:
These commands ship with the plugin:

Command What it does /harness:init [flags] Runs this installer non-interactively for the current project. No args → auto-detect stack, all components (warn mode), committed enablement. Pass through any installer flag (--stack, --components, --local, --no-plugin, …). /harness:agents [--copy] [owner/repo] Brings a stack's agent bundle into .claude/agents/. No args → the stack's default bundle (e.g. Rails → octanelabsdev/rails-agents), symlinked and gitignored (per-developer). --copy commits real files (whole team). Pass owner/repo (or a git URL) to override the bundle. See agents.md. /harness:status Inventory of what's loaded/configured in this project (components, stack profile, agents, MCP, bookshelf, session markers). /harness:doctor Deterministic health check — verifies hooks, tool scripts, schema, and config are present and wired. For a stack with a user-scope MCP server (rails), it also warns when the server isn't configured at user scope, the app isn't in the server's projects.yml, or a project .mcp.json entry runs it through bundle exec. Exits non-zero on a gap (CI/pre-push safe). /harness:update [--apply] Checks whether a newer release tag exists (read-only by default). With --apply, bumps this project's pinned ref to the latest tag; then run /plugin marketplace update harness and /reload-plugins to activate. See Updating.

docs.title: Updating
docs.text:
Stack / components. Re-run install.sh (it merges, preserving your other settings keys) or edit .claude/harness.json directly.

The pinned plugin version. The harness is a third-party marketplace, so Claude Code does not auto-update a ref-pinned marketplace — that's the point (a moving ref would let any push to the harness repo run on every machine at next session). Bumping from, say, v0.2.0 to v0.3.0 means changing the pinned ref in the settings.json that declares the marketplace. The settings source is authoritative — but /reload-plugins alone does not re-fetch the marketplace clone at the new tag; the old version keeps loading until /plugin marketplace update pulls it (observed moving 0.2.1 → 0.2.2). So the update is:

/harness:update                      # check: installed vs latest release tag (read-only)
/harness:update --apply              # bump the pinned ref (+sha) in settings to the latest tag
/plugin marketplace update harness   # fetch the marketplace at the newly pinned tag
/reload-plugins                      # load it
/harness:update                      # confirm: should report up to date

/plugin marketplace update fetches whatever ref settings currently pins — on its own it does not move you to a newer tag; the --apply bump is what crosses tags.

Cutting a release (maintainers). Merge a PR that bumps .claude-plugin/plugin.json and the README pin to the new version, pull main, then:

tools/release.sh v0.3.0 notes.md   # notes file optional; without it GitHub generates the notes

It refuses unless HEAD is origin/main with a clean tree, both files name the version, and tools/ci.sh is green. Then it pushes an annotated tag on HEAD, creates the GitHub Release marked Latest, deploys the docs, and confirms GitHub's latest release is the new tag. Each step is skipped when it's already done, so a failed run can be re-run; a tag already on another commit is never moved. The GitHub Release matters beyond the changelog: the docs header shows GitHub's latest release, so a tag without one leaves the site on the old version. It needs git, jq, gh (authenticated) and uv.

A fleet of repos. tools/fleet_repin.sh opens one re-pin PR per repo. List the repos in a file, one per line, with the branch the PR should target. The base branch is required, not guessed:

# ~/.config/harness/fleet.txt
~/dev/storefront   main
~/dev/billing      develop

~/harness/tools/fleet_repin.sh v0.3.0 ~/.config/harness/fleet.txt

For each repo it:

  • works in a detached temporary worktree off origin/<base>, so your checkout's files, branches and current branch are left alone (the PR branch exists only on origin);
  • pins ref to the tag and sha to the tag's commit, resolved with git ls-remote (an unknown tag stops the run before any repo is touched);
  • commits and pushes under the repo's own Ruby (.ruby-version, or ruby in .tool-versions, via mise exec), so Ruby git hooks load the right gems; a Ruby that isn't installed fails that repo;
  • opens the PR only after ls-remote shows the pushed commit on origin, then reads the pin back from the PR head on GitHub;
  • skips a repo whose base branch already pins the tag and sha.

Branches are named chore/harness-<tag>-<sha7>; an existing one on origin fails that repo rather than being reused. A failed repo is reported and the rest still run (exit 1). Running CI and merging the PRs are separate steps. It needs git, jq, gh (authenticated) and, for Ruby repos, mise.

Without PRs, the installer rewrites a checkout's pin in place: ~/harness/install.sh --ref v0.3.0 --yes /path/to/repo.

What the pin actually guarantees (ref, and the sha caveat). A ref pin freezes the marketplace at that tag's commit and disables auto-update — verified. The installer also records the tag's commit sha (--no-sha opts out; --sha SHA sets it explicitly), but only the ref is observably enforced through the settings→startup reconcile — the sha did not propagate to the machine cache in testing. So the effective guarantee is tag-level, not commit-level: a force-re-cut tag upstream could be pulled on the next reload. Protect your release tags (and the account: 2FA, branch/tag protection) — that, not the sha, is the real supply-chain mitigation. A branch/channel ref (main, stable) is left at ref-only so it can still move.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
/plugin disable harness@harness        # stop the hooks/skills
/plugin uninstall harness@harness      # remove it
Then delete .claude/harness.json and the harness keys from .claude/settings.json if you want it fully gone.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: bash, git, jq, python3 on PATH (the installer and hooks use them). ruby only if you use the story-writer's DoR lint.

docs.title: The banner says harness: NOT configured
docs.text: There's no .claude/harness.json in the project (or you're above the repo root). Run ~/harness/install.sh . in the project. The plugin can be enabled but the enforcing gates stay inert until the config exists — that's by design.

docs.title: The banner doesn't appear at all
docs.text:
• The plugin isn't picked up yet — restart Claude Code (or run /config once) after installing.
  • Confirm it's enabled: claude plugin list should show harness@harness … enabled.
  • Confirm the marketplace is known: claude plugin marketplace list.

docs.title: claude plugin install / marketplace add can't find it
docs.text: The marketplace is the public repo. Use octanelabsdev/harness (GitHub shorthand) or the full URL. Behind a proxy/firewall, ensure github.com is reachable.

docs.title: Marketplace harness is added but ignored in every repo
docs.text: claude plugin list shows harness@harness … failed to load with "Its source doesn't match its extraKnownMarketplaces entry in user or managed settings". The harness entry in your user settings (~/.claude/settings.json) has a ref/sha that the marketplace wasn't added with, so Claude Code ignores the marketplace everywhere. Remove ref and sha from that user entry, leaving {"source": "github", "repo": "octanelabsdev/harness"}, then restart. Pin versions in each project's .claude/settings.json, not in user settings. Before v0.2.16, /harness:update --apply could write that user entry when run from a worktree whose project settings file isn't tracked.

docs.title: Gates aren't firing
docs.text:
• Check .claude/harness.json → components: the gate must be true. The two gates default off when unconfigured.
  • Check the path you edited is under stack.impl_dirs — only the implementation surface is gated.
  • Confirm jq is installed (the hooks parse config with it).

docs.title: The verification gate never mentions operator tests
docs.text: That check needs both stack.ui_dirs (non-empty) and stack.operator_test_dir (non-empty). Stacks with no UI layer (e.g. generic, go) intentionally skip it. Also note: git collapses a fully untracked directory to one entry (app/), which can hide file-level granularity — commit a placeholder so new files show individually.

docs.title: Hooks seem to fire twice
docs.text: You probably have hooks in both a committed settings.json and the plugin (or an old $HOME-path hook left behind). Remove the old "hooks" block from settings.json; the plugin provides them. (This is exactly the migration the harness replaces — see the project's cleanup notes.)

docs.title: A teammate checked out the repo and nothing happened
docs.text: Enabling a plugin per-project takes effect when they trust the folder and restart. If you used --local, the enablement is in your gitignored settings.local.json and teammates won't get it — use project scope (default) for team-wide, or have each teammate run install.sh.

docs.title: ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} shows up literally
docs.text: It's substituted by Claude Code in plugin content (skills/agents) and set as a real env var for hook processes — but it is not expanded in ad-hoc Bash you run yourself. If you're testing a hook by hand, run it as Claude Code would (it sets the variable), or substitute the path manually.

docs.title: Work vs. personal configs are mixing
docs.text: The harness honors CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR. Launch work sessions with your work config (e.g. CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR=~/.claude-work claude) — the banner will report the work global ruleset, and the plugin cache/config stay under that home. The two never cross-read.

docs.title: Agents show as BROKEN in the banner
docs.text: Broken symlinks in .claude/agents/ — usually a bundle moved or an agent was renamed/removed. Re-link them (see agents.md).

docs.title: I want the gates to actually block, not warn
docs.text:
• Pipeline gate: touch .claude/.pipeline-block.
  • Verification gate: edit hooks/verification_gate.sh per the note at its tail (swap exit 0 for exit 2 when warnings exist). Promote only after the warn phase is quiet on false positives.

docs.title: The verification gate says UNVERIFIED or SETUP ERROR
docs.text: The suite didn't run to completion, so the gate refuses to pass it. - "another test run held the lock": another session or worktree of this repo was running the suite for longer than stack.test_lock_wait_sec. Let it finish, or raise the wait. - "exceeded …s and was killed": the suite is slower than stack.test_timeout_sec. Raise it; it's capped to fit the Stop hook's 1800s timeout. - SETUP ERROR: one of those settings isn't whole seconds, or the lock file can't be created in the repo's git dir. - "no tests ran": the command passed, but every test summary in its output said 0 tests (0 runs,, 0 tests, or 0 examples,). The command doesn't match the suite, e.g. bin/rails test in an RSpec app. Set stack.test_command to "auto" or the right command; /harness:doctor shows what the gate will run.

docs.title: The verification gate fails with Bundler::GemNotFound or the wrong Ruby
docs.text: Hooks inherit Claude Code's environment, which can carry a different Ruby than the repo's .ruby-version. When mise has that Ruby installed, the gate runs the suite under mise exec ruby@<.ruby-version> --; if you use mise for Ruby, run mise install so it does. Otherwise the gate uses whatever Ruby the environment provides; rbenv's shims read .ruby-version themselves. /harness:doctor says which applies.

docs.title: The rails MCP server won't connect (-32602 Unsupported protocol version)
docs.text:
Installers before v0.2.7 wrote a project .mcp.json running bundle exec rails-mcp-server and suggested gem "rails-mcp-server" in the Gemfile. A project entry overrides your user-scope rails server, and on a legacy Rails app (e.g. Rails 7.0 / rack 2.2) bundler can only resolve rails-mcp-server 1.0.1, because every protocol-compatible release (1.2.0+ switched to fast-mcp; 1.6.1/2.0.0 need newer activesupport) conflicts with the app's locked deps. 1.0.1 → mcp-rb 0.3.2 speaks only MCP protocol 2024-11-05 and hard-rejects the newer version Claude Code offers instead of negotiating down — so the handshake dies with -32602.

Don't try the mise shim (~/.local/share/mise/shims/rails-mcp-server) as a fix: it's cwd-sensitive and, launched from the project dir, resolves to the same broken in-bundle 1.0.1 (its version output from $HOME is misleading).

Fix — one standalone server at user scope, by absolute path. rails-mcp-server is a standalone tool: it reads ~/.config/rails-mcp/projects.yml and introspects by shelling into the target app's own bin/rails, so it never needs to be in the app bundle.

  1. Install a current version outside any bundle (gem install rails-mcp-server under a modern Ruby, or via mise global), then add it once per machine: claude mcp add --scope user rails -- /absolute/path/to/rails-mcp-server --mode stdio (re-running the installer prints this line with the path filled in).
  2. In the app: delete the rails entry from .mcp.json (the whole file if it was the only one) and gem "rails-mcp-server" from the Gemfile, then bundle install.
  3. Re-run the installer (or add <name>: "/path/to/app" to projects.yml yourself) and restart Claude Code. /harness:doctor should report the user-scope server and the registration, with no override warning.

2.0.0 (fast-mcp) negotiates the handshake and Claude Code connects.

docs.title: The docs header shows an older version
docs.text: The version next to the repo link is GitHub's latest release, not the latest tag. A tag pushed without a GitHub Release leaves it on the previous one; tools/release.sh creates both (see Install). The browser also caches it per tab, so after a release open the site in a new tab; a refresh keeps the old value.

docs.title: Validate a change to the harness itself
docs.text:
claude plugin validate . --strict
Runs the marketplace/plugin/skill checks. Use --strict in CI to fail on warnings.

docs.title: Choosing a lane
docs.text:
Every piece of work goes through one of two lanes. Pick the lightest one that fits. Ceremony that doesn't match the size of the change gets skipped, and a skipped gate teaches everyone to skip gates.

If the work is… Lane Guide A typo, a copy change, a config tweak, a one-line fix Small fix A small fix One feature or bug you could describe in a paragraph, done in a day or two Story A story

Bigger than one story? Split it into stories, one per piece you could ship on its own.

docs.title: The tools, and when they come into play
docs.text:
You ask for these:

Say… Tool When "What should I work on next?" product-manager You sit down and don't know where to start "Write this up as a story" story-writer Before building anything that isn't a small fix "Blind-review this" blind-review A story is built and the tests are green "Check the books on …" bookshelf A design or idiom call you'd like grounded in a source /harness:status, /harness:doctor commands Something feels off: a gate didn't fire, a plugin didn't load

These run on their own; you only notice them:

  • Session banner: what's actually configured, at the start of every session.
  • Guardrails: short checklists Claude loads before an edit, after a failure and before saying "done".
  • Pipeline gate: warns (or blocks) when feature code changes without a ready story or a small-fix marker.
  • Stop gate: runs your tests at the end of every turn that changed code. A red suite keeps the turn going.
  • Review gate (if on): a turn can't end without a passing review of the current code.

Your override: touch .claude/.verification-warn turns the Stop gate into a warning for this checkout. Use it when you knowingly accept a red suite, such as a flaky test against an outside service. It's a human decision, never Claude's. Delete the file to turn the gate back on.

docs.title: A week, for example
docs.text: Day Repo Work Lane Monday Trailhead (a booking app) A customer reports a wrong tax total Story: write it up, build, blind-review, commit Tuesday Trailhead A typo in the footer Small fix Wednesday Riverbend visitor guide Add the events calendar Story Thursday Riverbend visitor guide The contact page lists the wrong opening hours Small fix Friday Trailhead Not sure what's next "What should I work on next?"

docs.title: A small fix
docs.text: For changes too small to need a story: a typo, a copy change, a config value, an obvious one-line bug. If you'd have to explain the change in more than a sentence, it's a story.

docs.title: Example: a typo in Trailhead's booking confirmation
docs.text:
The confirmation email says "Your reservaton is confirmed."

1. Declare it. Write one line saying what and why:

printf '%s\n' 'Fix "reservaton" typo in the booking confirmation email' > .claude/.small-fix

The pipeline gate lets edits through while this file exists, and it repeats the line on every edit so the bypass stays visible. touch .claude/.small-fix also works; the line just makes the reason show.

2. Ask.

You: The booking confirmation email says "reservaton". Fix it.

3. Let the Stop gate run. The tests still run when the turn ends. A one-line change can break a test like any other: a mailer test that asserts the exact subject line, for instance. Red keeps the turn going until it's fixed.

4. Commit, then remove the marker.

rm .claude/.small-fix

Leaving it in place lets the next feature skip its story without anyone noticing.

docs.title: When it isn't a small fix
docs.text:
Stop and switch to a story when:

  • the fix needs a decision ("should cancelled bookings get this email too?");
  • it touches more than one behaviour;
  • you find yourself writing a new test for new behaviour, not adjusting one.

docs.title: A story
docs.text: For one feature or one bug with clear edges: something you could describe in a paragraph and finish in a day or two. Bigger than that, or several pieces that only work together: split it into stories, one per piece you could ship on its own.

docs.title: Example: Trailhead shows the wrong tax total
docs.text: A customer reports that a two-night booking shows tax for one night.

docs.title: 1. Decide (skip if you already know)
docs.text:
You: What should I work on next?

product-manager reads the board's real signals (pinned, blocking, priority, age) and proposes the top item. Here it's the tax bug, because it's pinned and two other cards wait on it.

docs.title: 2. Write it up
docs.text:
You: Write this up as a story.

story-writer turns the report into a Definition-of-Ready card: what's in, what's out, acceptance criteria. Where the report is silent, it asks instead of guessing:

Claude: Is tax charged per night or per booking? The report doesn't say, and the code does both in different places.

You: Per night, at the rate on the booking date.

Answer these yourself. An open question answered by a guess is how the wrong thing gets built correctly. The card passes a deterministic lint and is recorded at .claude/current-story.yaml, which is what unlocks the pipeline gate.

docs.title: 3. Build
docs.text:
You: Build it.

Claude (through your agents, if the project has them) writes a failing test for the reported case, then the fix. When the turn ends, the Stop gate runs your tests. Red keeps the turn going:

VERIFICATION GATE — test_command failed: bin/rails test
BookingTest#test_two_night_tax: expected 24.0, got 12.0

Your job here is light: glance at the diff, answer questions.

docs.title: 4. Review
docs.text:
You: Blind-review this.

The reviewer gets the diff and the project's rules, but not the story or the conversation, so it judges the code on its own terms. Critical findings go back for a fix, then it reviews again. With review_gate on, a turn can't end on a stale or failing review, and any edit after the review makes it stale.

docs.title: 5. Commit
docs.text: Tests green and review passed: commit. Committing doesn't make the review stale; editing does.

docs.title: Signs it's bigger than one story
docs.text:
• The story-writer keeps finding open questions that need someone else's answer.
  • One story turns into "and then we also need…" three times.

Split it: one story per piece you could ship on its own, with the open questions settled before you write the next one.
